prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Strapped to the bed of circumcision lies My son. This mutilation ties You to the fathers. They will never let You forget, or your flesh be enfranchised ever, Though you pray all your life long. They set you early on the rack, infect you with a fever Of remembering. In the marriage bed, When you are naked, there the sign is red. There is neither meeting nor mating but the past Cries that you've been waited for and wed already— I will not bless this mark upon your body. For you the hurricane is rising fast; I feel the horns of Moses in my head And Law wrenched again from the dead Hand of deity, and I descend out of the blast to you Mad with loneliness upon this bed. But I reserve also the rage That broke the Law upon you like a rain of stone That other time I saw you so could yearn. The Law is broken, baby. I will not ascend again.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Strapped, This, You

outputs.L1:
Strapped to the bed of circumcision lies my son.  
This mutilation binds you to the fathers.  
They will never let you forget,  
nor will your flesh ever be enfranchised,  
though you pray all your life long.

They set you early upon the rack,  
infecting you with the fever of remembrance.  
In the marriage bed,  
when you are naked,  
there the sign remains red.  
There is neither meeting nor mating  
but the past cries out  
that you have been awaited  
and already wed.

I will not bless this mark upon your body.  
For you, the hurricane is rising fast;  
I feel the horns of Moses in my head,  
and the Law wrenched once more  
from the dead hand of deity.  
I descend out of the blast to you,  
mad with loneliness upon this bed.

Yet I reserve also the rage  
that broke the Law upon you  
like a rain of stone—  
that other time I saw you so could yearn.  
The Law is broken, baby.  
I will not ascend again.
outputs.L2:
My child is lying on the circumcision bed, bound in place.  
This cutting makes you part of the lineage of the ancestors.  
They will make sure you can never escape that inheritance,  
and your body will never be fully free from it,  
no matter how many prayers you offer throughout your life.  

From the beginning, they fasten you to suffering  
and plant in you a burning illness of memory.  
Later, in the bed of marriage,  
when you stand exposed, the mark will still be visible.  
No encounter, no act of love, will be untouched by history:  
the past will cry out that you were expected, claimed,  
and already joined to it before any human union.  

I refuse to give my blessing to that wound on your body.  
For your sake, a storm is gathering with terrible speed.  
I feel the horns of Moses pressing inside my mind,  
and I feel the Law being torn once more  
from the lifeless hand of God.  
Out of that violent wind I come down to you,  
crazed with solitude, finding you here on this bed.  

Yet I also keep within me the fury  
that once shattered the Law over you  
like a shower of stones,  
when I saw you before and recognized such longing in you.  
The Law has been broken, my child.  
I will not climb back up again.
outputs.L3:
The speaker presents circumcision not as a sacred rite, but as a form of mutilation imposed on the child before he can consent. Rather than viewing the act as a blessing or a meaningful entrance into religious community, the speaker sees it as a violent inscription of ancestral law onto the child’s body. The mark becomes a physical sign of tradition, inheritance, and obedience, binding the child permanently to a history and authority he has not chosen for himself.

The poem suggests that this bodily mark will not remain confined to the moment of ritual. It will follow the child throughout his life, entering his adulthood, his memories, his intimate relationships, and his sense of identity. The body becomes a place where history is stored, and the scar becomes a reminder of the power that family, religion, and tradition have exercised over him. In this way, the poem treats circumcision as both a physical wound and a symbolic burden.

Because of this, the speaker refuses to bless or accept what has been done to the child’s body. The refusal is not merely personal; it is a rejection of the values and religious structures that present the act as holy or necessary. The speaker cannot transform the wound into a sign of covenant or belonging. Instead, the mark remains, in the speaker’s eyes, an injury—one that cannot be justified by appeals to custom, faith, or ancestral command.

The poem intensifies this rejection by invoking Moses and the breaking of the Law. Moses, traditionally associated with divine commandment and religious authority, becomes a figure through whom the speaker expresses anger at inherited law itself. The breaking of the Law suggests rebellion against a tradition that demands obedience even at the cost of bodily harm. By drawing on this biblical imagery, the speaker turns the language of religion against religious authority, using it to voice rage rather than reverence.

At the end of the poem, the speaker rejects the idea of returning to divine law or submitting again to inherited commandments. Instead of accepting the authority of tradition, the speaker chooses to remain with the child—with his vulnerability, his wounded body, and his human reality. This final choice shifts the poem away from obedience to God or ancestry and toward compassion, protection, and presence. The speaker’s loyalty is not to the Law, but to the child who has been marked by it.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents infant circumcision not as a sacred blessing, but as an inherited act of religious and cultural violence imposed on a child before he can consent. Framed as a dramatic address from a parent to a son, it transforms what tradition might call a covenant into a wound, a bodily inscription through which the past lays claim to the future. The speaker resists the idea that ancestry, scripture, or communal obligation can justify marking the child’s body in the name of belonging.

Biblical imagery gives the poem much of its force. References to Moses, the Law, and covenant evoke the authority of religious tradition, but the poem turns that authority against itself. Instead of presenting the Law as holy, protective, or life-giving, the speaker sees it as broken, violent, and unworthy of obedience. The inherited commandment becomes a burden passed down through generations, and the child’s body becomes the place where that burden is enforced.

At the center of the poem is a fierce parental refusal. The speaker will not bless the act, will not soften it with ritual language, and will not allow it to be understood as love simply because it has been sanctioned by tradition. The mark of circumcision is imagined as a lifelong claim made by the dead, the ancestors, and the old religious order upon the living child. Against that claim, the poem asserts the parent’s responsibility to protect the child from inherited harm.

By declaring the Law broken, the poem rejects the moral authority of the tradition that demands the cut. Its tone is defiant, grief-stricken, and accusatory, shaped by anger at a culture that confuses obedience with holiness and injury with identity. Ultimately, the poem becomes an act of resistance: a refusal to perpetuate violence in the name of covenant, and a demand that the child’s body belong first to himself rather than to history, religion, or ancestral command.

This is the moment when you realize how much strength you have. You may feel strapped by responsibilities, deadlines, or expectations, but that does not mean you are stuck forever. Every challenge can teach you something about patience, courage, and resilience.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark free-verse dramatic monologue from a mother watching her infant son being circumcised, using biblical imagery of Moses, law, ancestry, rage, and alienation.
counterfactuals.output:
I held you down for the covenant.

Forgive me.

No—
do not forgive me yet.

Let the room remember
how your mouth opened
like a little Red Sea,
how the cry came through you
as if God had leaned over the cradle
and blown wrath into your lungs.

They said: law.

They said: eighth day.

They said: Abraham,
and I saw old men rising in the wallpaper,
bearded with dust,
hands smelling of ram and desert,
nodding from behind the fluorescent lights.

They said: son of your people.

But you were only my son,
slick with milk,
warm as bread,
your fists closed around nothing
as if nothing were an inheritance
worth keeping.

I wanted to be Zipporah
with the flint in her hand,
the blood at the feet,
the terrible wife who knew
how to barter with an angel.

I wanted to seize Moses by the beard
and ask him
what kind of God waits in the road
to murder a child
unless a mother becomes a knife.

But I stood there.

I stood there while the law
put on gloves.

I stood there while ancestry
entered the room
not as song,
not as Sabbath candles,
not as my grandmother’s trembling blessing,
but as a clamp,
a bright instrument,
a commandment with no face.

My rage had nowhere holy to go.

It struck the ceiling.
It struck my own ribs.
It circled you like a starving dog.

And all the fathers in my blood said:
This is how he belongs.

Belongs to whom?

To the desert that never nursed him?
To the scroll that never woke at 3 a.m.
with breasts aching?
To the tribe that will one day
measure his manhood
by what was taken
before he could say his name?

You cried,
and the sound split me
from Egypt to Sinai.

I was Pharaoh.
I was slave.
I was the river full of baskets.
I was the mother hiding the child
and the mother surrendering him.
I was Miriam in the reeds,
watching power lift him away.

And you—
my small, red, furious prophet—
you preached without words
against all of us.

Against the fathers.
Against the God of fathers.
Against me.

Especially me.

Afterward they wrapped you,
declared you clean,
declared you entered,
declared the ancient door opened.

But your eyes found mine
with that newborn blindness,
that dark milk-blue accusation,
and I knew:

some doors are mouths.

Some blessings bite.

Some laws come down the mountain
already smoking
with the smell of burned sons.

I took you back into my arms
as if arms could undo history.

I rocked you
under the names of the dead.

I whispered the name we gave you,
trying to make it larger than the wound,
larger than the covenant,
larger than the God
who keeps asking mothers
to prove their faith
with the bodies of their children.

Sleep, I said.

But I did not mean sleep.

I meant:
return.

Return to before the blade,
before the book,
before the fathers named your flesh
a borderland.

Return to the waters.

Return to me.

And if Moses comes again
out of the dark corridor,
law in one hand,
stone in the other,

I will not bow.

I will stand between him and the cradle
with milk on my gown
and murder in my heart,

and I will say:

Enough desert.

Enough blood.

This child is not your promised land.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the voice of a Jewish mother rejecting the ritual circumcision of her baby, framing it as inherited trauma and a violent covenant with the fathers.
counterfactuals.output:
I will not hand you over  
to the trembling knife  
because my father’s father’s father  
called pain a doorway  
and named the blood “belonging.”

I have heard the old story:  
a man lifting his son  
toward a God who asked too much,  
the ram appearing late,  
the boy learning early  
that love may arrive  
with rope in its hands.

They say covenant.  
I hear commandment  
echoing through men  
who were once babies,  
who became fathers,  
who forgot the first language  
of their own skin.

My son, you sleep  
with your fists like unopened figs,  
your whole body a yes  
no one has asked to alter.  
You are already marked—  
by breath, by milk,  
by the dark soft crown  
I kiss in the night.

Let the fathers gather  
with their ancient blades,  
their blessings sharp as flint.  
Let them say I am breaking  
the chain.

I say: some chains  
are meant to end  
in a mother’s hands.

I will give you Hebrew songs,  
candles cupped against dusk,  
the taste of honey,  
the stubborn questions,  
the wrestle with angels,  
the names of the dead  
spoken into light.

But not this wound.  
Not this inheritance  
wrapped in gauze.  
Not this violence  
called welcome.

If there is a covenant  
between God and my child,  
let it be written  
in laughter first,  
in choice,  
in the body kept whole  
until he can open  
his own mouth  
and answer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a confessional poem about circumcision as a mark of religious law on the body, with intense imagery involving marriage, memory, Moses, broken tablets, and maternal fury.
counterfactuals.output:
I was eight days old when the covenant  
found me sleeping.

A blade, a blessing, my mother’s face  
white as milk left out beneath the moon—  
and all the women whispering law  
as if law were a cradle,  
as if blood could be taught to sing.

I do not remember the pain,  
which is the first lie memory tells.  
I remember it anyway:  
a red door opening in the body,  
my name tied there like a ribbon,  
God leaning close with His old hunger.

Later I learned Moses carried stone  
down from the mountain—  
letters burning in his arms—  
and broke them at the sight of us  
dancing, glittering, faithless, alive.  
All my life I have felt those tablets  
shatter inside me:  
commandment becoming gravel,  
gravel becoming teeth.

What is a man  
but a marriage between wound and witness?  
What is a husband  
but someone who brings his scar to the bed  
and calls it inheritance?

On my wedding night  
I thought of Zipporah, furious and swift,  
flinging the foreskin at Moses’ feet—  
bridegroom of blood, she named him,  
and I understood at last  
that some mothers save their children  
by raging against heaven.

My mother never spoke of it.  
But I have seen her hands  
fold napkins like burial cloths,  
seen her eyes go black  
when the rabbi praised obedience.  
Inside her silence lived a lioness  
pacing the nursery,  
ready to tear the angels from the walls.

O law carved into flesh,  
O small altar I did not choose,  
O memory before memory—  
you have followed me  
through bathwater, prayer, desire,  
through every mirror where the body asks  
who signed this covenant  
on my behalf.

And still I carry it:  
not proudly, not only in shame,  
but as one carries a fragment  
of a broken tablet—  
sharp, holy, impossible to throw away,  
warm from the hand  
that smashed it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Sylvia Plath–like poem where a mother addresses her son during circumcision, blending tenderness, horror, biblical symbolism, and rebellion against patriarchal tradition.
counterfactuals.output:
**Little Covenant**

My milk-white son,  
laid out under the lamp’s small sun,  
you are not Isaac,  
though the old men have brought their knives  
and their God with the iron beard.

Your fist opens—  
a pink anemone in the antiseptic weather—  
then shuts on nothing.  
O furious pearl,  
O rabbit-heart kicking in its cotton burrow,  
forgive me.

They say this is a door  
cut into the body,  
a signature of fathers,  
a bright obedience.  
They say blood remembers  
what women must not question.

But I remember too.

I remember Sarah’s laugh  
curdled in the tent,  
Zipporah with the flint,  
her hand red as sunrise,  
flinging the foreskin at the feet  
of the devouring angel—  
bridegroom of blood,  
bridegroom of blood—  
and every mother since  
taught to call the wound holy.

Your cry climbs the room  
like a ladder on fire.  
The nurse smiles,  
the rabbi murmurs,  
the silver instrument shines  
with its neat little moon of appetite.

My darling,  
I would swaddle the world  
in my own skin for you.  
I would bite the serpent’s head  
and spit out Eden’s law.  
I would unname the fathers,  
unwrite the book,  
tear the covenant like a black cloth  
from the altar.

Yet here you are,  
small king without a kingdom,  
marked before speech,  
entered into history  
through pain’s narrow gate.

Hush now.  
My mouth is a dark house  
full of bees.  
My arms are the only commandments  
I trust.

Sleep, little rebel.  
Let the blood dry.  
Let the old God count his coins.

You are mine—  
not as property,  
not as proof,  
not as a lamb.

Mine as the dawn is mine  
when it breaks,  
refusing every knife  
that named the night sacred.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a bleak, prophetic poem in which the speaker refuses to bless her son’s circumcision and imagines herself descending like Moses from the mountain to break the Law forever.
counterfactuals.output:
**Tablets**

They brought him to me swaddled  
in the white weather of women—  
milk-breath, salt-skin,  
his fists still closed around nothing  
as if nothing were a kingdom  
he had not yet learned to lose.

The men waited with their knives  
bright as small moons.  
Their prayers climbed the walls  
and clung there, black insects  
warming themselves  
on the name of God.

They said: Bless him.

But my mouth was a cave  
after the fire had gone out.  
My tongue lay in ashes.  
I had no amen left  
for the covenant of blood,  
no song for the first wound  
made holy by being inherited.

My son slept,  
that blind prophet of the cradle,  
and in his dream  
the whole desert opened—  
forty years of fathers  
dragging their sons by the hand  
toward a promised blade.

I saw the mountain then,  
its skull of stone  
split by thunder.  
I saw the Law  
held up like lightning  
in the hands of a man  
too dazzled to disobey.

But I was not dazzled.

I took the tablets  
from the burning height,  
not to carry them down  
but to let them fall.

I descended through smoke,  
through the old terrified music,  
through the camps of obedience,  
where mothers covered their faces  
and called it faith.

Below me the people danced  
around every golden commandment,  
every god hammered  
from fear and hunger.  
They lifted their children  
like offerings to history.  
They called the knife a door.  
They called the scar a seal.  
They called surrender  
belonging.

I came down with the storm  
caught in my hair.  
I came down barren of blessing.  
I came down saying No  
until the word grew antlers,  
until it gored the altar,  
until the heavens themselves  
stepped back.

And when I reached them  
I raised the Law above my head—  
that ancient stone,  
that alphabet of wound and will—  
and broke it.

Not once,  
but forever.

The shards flew out  
like black birds  
over the tents,  
over the knives,  
over the sleeping boys  
whose bodies had been promised  
before they had breath  
to refuse.

Let the desert remember this:  
a mother’s silence  
can become a plague.  
A mother’s grief  
can unmake a god.  
A mother’s hand  
can take the chisel  
from the angel  
and grind the commandment  
back into dust.

They said: Bless him.

I gathered my son  
against my breast,  
his whole body unbroken,  
his future dark and warm  
beneath my palm.

I did not bless the blade.

I blessed the flesh  
that had not yet learned  
to forgive us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
